query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys subjected to tribo-corrosion, repeated mechanical wear disrupts the naturally forming protective oxide/passivating film, exposing microstructurally heterogeneous regions that act as micro-galvanic couples. This disruption accelerates localized corrosion at interfaces between phases of differing nobility, thereby governing the coupled degradation response.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-processed HEA with a dual-phase microstructure (e.g., a primary BCC matrix with secondary precipitates such as Laves phases) that normally forms a thin, protective, passivating oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Applying controlled, cyclic mechanical wear (tribological contacts) concurrently with exposure to a corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl aqueous solution), compared to a static corrosion test without wear.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at room temperature in identical corrosive media, where one set of samples undergoes wear-corrosion cycles and the baseline set is only exposed to the corrosive medium without mechanical disruption.
generation.structural_mediator: The heterogeneous microstructure (different phases with varied passive film stability) acting as the sites for micro-galvanic coupling when the protective oxide is mechanically removed.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear continuously removes the passivating oxide layer, exposing fresh alloy surfaces with contrasting electrochemical potentials. These differences lead to localized micro-galvanic cells that accelerate corrosion at phase boundaries, thereby coupling the wear and corrosion processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline static corrosion condition, samples subjected to tribo-corrosion will exhibit a higher total degradation rate marked by both increased wear track depths and a higher density/depth of corrosion pits. The combined effect should exceed the sum of isolated wear and corrosion, owing to the accelerated corrosion from galvanic coupling.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy samples exposed solely to the corrosive medium with the opportunity to re-establish a passivating oxide layer (static corrosion condition).
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in environments where a passive oxide film typically forms (e.g., aqueous NaCl solutions) and where the wear rate is sufficient to disrupt the oxide. It may fail or be less pronounced in environments with inherently nonpassivating conditions (e.g., certain molten salts) or when wear is negligible compared to the film reformation rate.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative acceleration factors of corrosion due to wear-induced film disruption are uncertain, as they depend on the balance between the wear frequency/intensity and the kinetics of passive film reformation, as well as on the specific compositional heterogeneities of the HEA.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA samples with the described dual-phase microstructure. One set is subjected to controlled cyclic wear in a corrosive 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, while the control set is immersed in the same NaCl solution under quiescent conditions. Monitor the evolution of surface morphology via microscopy, quantify corrosion pit density and depth, measure wear track profiles, and evaluate overall material loss over time.
measurements: Microscopic analysis of corrosion pits and interfacial regions (SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tribo-corrosion samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in localized corrosion (e.g., pit density/depth) or overall material loss beyond the additive effects of wear and static corrosion observed in the baseline samples, then the hypothesis that wear-induced passive film disruption accelerates micro-galvanic corrosion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. The average hardness of the WVTaTiCr alloy coating reaches 627.36 HV. After 50 h of high-temperature oxidation, the oxide weight of WVTaTiCr increases by 5.12 m

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
